title: Sorting & Pattern
strapline: Grouping the world and spotting what comes next.
intent: Sorting is the very foundation of mathematical thinking — noticing how things are the same and different and grouping them.
Making and continuing patterns builds the sense of sequence and prediction that underpins number, reading and music.
Handling and arranging real, interesting objects keeps the maths concrete, hands-on and playful.
Deciding your own rule for sorting — and explaining it — is genuine reasoning and problem-solving.
It's naturally rich in comparing talk — same, different, bigger, more, next, because.
implementation: Offer collections worth sorting — buttons, shells, keys, bottle tops, natural finds — in trays and hoops.
Let children invent their own sorting rules before you suggest any: 'How have you decided to group these?'
Model making a simple pattern and pausing: 'Red, blue, red, blue... what do you think comes next?'
Name the thinking out loud: 'You've put all the shiny ones together — you sorted by shine!'
Stretch it gently: sort the same collection a different way, or make the pattern longer or trickier.
Take it into everyday routines — tidying by type, sorting the snack, threading a repeating necklace.
Add pattern-making across the areas: printing, beads, music, movement, building.
key_questions: How have you sorted these — what's your rule?
Could you sort the same things a different way?
What comes next in your pattern — how do you know?
Which group has more? How can we check?
What's the same, and what's different, about these two?

impact.text: Children sort and group objects by colour, size, shape and their own chosen rules.
Children copy, continue and create repeating patterns and can say what comes next.
Children match, compare and notice what is the same and different, explaining their thinking.
Children decide and explain their own sorting rules, reasoning about how things belong.
Children compare amounts across their groups using 'more', 'fewer' and 'the same'.
Children handle and arrange the objects with careful, controlled hands.

enhancements: Interesting collections to sort: buttons, keys, shells, bottle tops, pom-poms, natural finds.
Sorting trays, hoops and bowls, some labelled and some open-ended.
Beads, pegs and threading for making repeating patterns.
Pattern strips to copy and continue, and blanks to invent your own.
Everyday sorting jobs — tidying, matching socks, sorting the recycling.
Pattern-making in other areas: printing, music, movement and construction.

playing_exploring: Children explore collections freely, discovering how things can be grouped.
They test different ways of arranging and matching the objects.
active_learning: Children stay with a sorting or pattern challenge, absorbed in getting it just right.
creating_thinking: Children invent their own rules, predict what comes next, and explain their reasoning.
